title: Drake Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Drake wells have a 380-foot median depth, 5.0 gpm median yield, and estimated finished costs of $30,700-$50,000.
h1: Drake, Colorado Well Depths, Yields, and Costs
intro_html:
Buying land near Drake means dealing with mountain bedrock, not a predictable shallow groundwater basin. Records within 5 miles show a median well depth of 380 feet, a median reported yield of 5.0 gpm, and a wide range of results. Most permitted wells serve domestic or household use, and most are completed in unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers.

The permit record is useful for setting expectations, but it is not a guarantee for a particular lot. A nearby well can help a driller understand the local rock, while still producing a different result. Review well construction, pump-test, water-level, septic, and permit information before you commit to a property.

sections.heading: How deep are wells around Drake?
sections.html:
Drake wells have a 380-foot median depth. The middle half runs from 199 to 556 feet, so a bid based only on the median can be misleading. A quarter of reported wells are shallower than 199 feet, while another quarter exceed 556 feet. The deepest recorded well is 1,400 feet.

The depth mix shows the spread clearly: 39% are between 300 and 600 feet, 23% are 600 feet or deeper, and 14% are under 100 feet. Most permits identify unnamed fractured bedrock; smaller groups identify Fractured Crystalline and Fractured Granite. In this terrain, fractures control where water is found, so a driller should price the likely depth range rather than promise one exact depth.

sections.heading: What yield can a Drake well provide?
sections.html:
The median reported pump yield near Drake is 5.0 gpm, with the middle half between 4.2 and 7.0 gpm. That is a workable domestic range for many homes, but the well’s storage, pump setup, household demand, and any required water treatment still matter.

Reported results are concentrated in the 5-to-15-gpm range, which accounts for 70% of wells. Another 16% report 1 to 5 gpm, while 11% are under 1 gpm. Only 4% report more than 15 gpm. Ask for the actual well construction report and yield test, not just a neighbor’s verbal estimate. An exempt household-use well is generally limited to 35 gpm under Colorado rules, and the permit controls the allowed use.

sections.heading: What do water levels show in Drake?
sections.html:
Only 59 wells in the records report a static water level, so this part of the dataset is much smaller than the depth record. Among those reports, the median depth to water is 100 feet, with the middle half from 46 to 250 feet below the surface.

The decade comparison does not show a measured decline: the median static water level was 100 feet in both the 2010s and the 2020s. That is a stable result in this limited record, not a guarantee that water levels will be the same on your lot. Mountain wells can respond differently across short distances because fractures are uneven. Have a driller review nearby water levels, pumping information, and seasonal conditions when evaluating a parcel.

sections.heading: Who has drilled near Drake, and when?
sections.html:
Permit activity near Drake extends from the 1950s through 2025. The busiest decades were the 1990s, with 257 permits, and the 1970s, with 202. The records contain 1,144 wells, including 818 recorded as constructed. Permit counts describe the history of drilling, not the current availability or reputation of a contractor.

Ingram Drilling Inc., listed with Stephen E. Ingram, appears on 237 records. Hersh & Son Well Drilling Inc., listed with Harry Hersh, appears on 218, and High Desert Irrigation LLC, listed with Larry Hersh, appears on 149. Use those records to identify local experience, then verify licensing, insurance, scope, and references before hiring. A DWR permit and a completed construction report are separate things to confirm.

sections.heading: What does a new well cost near Drake?
sections.html:
Drake’s fractured granite and gneiss make depth the main cost driver. The local model uses $65-$100 per foot for drilling. At the 380-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $24,700-$38,000.

A finished system, including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, is estimated at $30,700-$50,000 at that median depth. Treat this as a planning range, not a fixed quote. The middle half of well depths runs from 199 to 556 feet, and some wells are much deeper. Ask what happens if the hole is dry or low-yield, whether casing and grout are included, and which site-access, power, storage, treatment, and trench conditions are excluded.

sections.heading: Risks to check before buying or building
sections.html:
The main physical risk is inconsistent fractured-bedrock production. The records show 11% of reported yields under 1 gpm, and a dry or weak hole can still require substantial drilling expense. Have the driller review neighboring wells, but do not assume one nearby result predicts your lot.

Water quality also deserves testing before closing and again after construction. Within about 10 miles are 9 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 40 historic mine features. There are no EPA Superfund or cleanup sites mapped in that search area. Those mapped sites do not prove contamination at a property, but they support checking source, drainage, and testing history. Septic setbacks, suitable soil, driveway access, electrical trenching, and building-site layout should be reviewed together with the well location.

sections.heading: A practical Drake lot-buying plan
sections.html:
Start with the Colorado DWR permit record for the parcel and neighboring properties. Confirm the permit type, permitted use, construction report, total depth, casing and grout details, pump yield, and any static water-level reading. Because 93% of permits are for domestic or household use, do not assume a domestic permit covers irrigation, commercial use, or additional residences.

Before you build, obtain a written drilling and completion estimate based on the lot’s access and likely depth range. Test existing water for the uses you plan, and have a septic professional verify the system location and soils. If the property is in an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be required for some uses. Compare Drake with nearby Glen Haven and Estes Park only as local context; the parcel’s own geology and legal water status control the decision.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Drake, Colorado?
faq.a: Within 5 miles of Drake, the median reported well depth is 380 feet. The middle half runs from 199 to 556 feet, while 23% of wells are 600 feet or deeper. The deepest record is 1,400 feet. Fractured mountain bedrock makes neighboring results useful for planning, but not a guarantee for a particular lot.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Drake?
faq.a: The median reported yield near Drake is 5.0 gpm, with the middle half between 4.2 and 7.0 gpm. Seventy percent of reported wells produce 5 to 15 gpm. However, 11% report less than 1 gpm. Review the well’s actual pump test, storage, and permitted use before assuming it can support a home or other demand.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Drake?
faq.a: The local drilling model is $65-$100 per foot. At Drake’s 380-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $24,700-$38,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work is estimated at $30,700-$50,000. A deeper, difficult, dry, or low-yield hole can change the final cost substantially.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Drake, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from a permit or a nearby well. Within about 10 miles, the records map 9 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 40 historic mine features. There are no EPA Superfund or cleanup sites mapped there. Test the property’s water for relevant contaminants, especially when mining features, drainage, or PFAS history may affect the site.

faq.q: Can I build a house on a well near Drake?
faq.a: Many local permits are for domestic or household use, accounting for 93% of the records, but the individual permit controls what is allowed. Before building, verify the DWR permit, well yield, water quality, septic feasibility, access, power, and trenching. If the planned use requires additional legal water in an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be necessary.
